headline: Roosters win the NRL Grand Final 19-18 in a thriller, while the ASX slipped 0.49% today and US tech rebounded last night on fading AI regulation fears.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS tracks the entire US share market, so it moves in sync with US stocks. Last night the NASDAQ bounced hard (+1.09%), but VTS closed lower today on the ASX — likely because the Aussie dollar fell sharply (-0.91%), which can affect how the AUD-priced ETF is repriced. The long-term US market story remains intact.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI held AI-focused global stocks, which have been under pressure after fears that incoming US Democrats plan to ramp up AI regulation. Despite the NASDAQ bouncing last night, the ASX-listed ETF closed down again today. This one is down -20% overall — the AI regulation overhang is the core drag right now.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG is a broad high-growth fund with heavy exposure to international shares. It dipped today broadly in line with the ASX and the weaker Aussie dollar repricing international holdings. No specific bad news — just market noise.

movers.name: BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF
movers.note: DHHF slipped today alongside the broader ASX dip of 0.49%. It tracks a mix of global and Australian shares, so a soft local session pulled it down slightly. Nothing structural — just a quiet down day.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dipped last night despite the broader NASDAQ rallying. Some profit-taking after recent strength, and there's an ongoing debate about whether big AI capital spending (like Microsoft's massive data centre build-out) will pay off. The long-term position is still up nearly 20% overall.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE had a good day today, rising 1.19%. Emerging markets got a lift, possibly as the Aussie dollar weakness and improved risk sentiment in Asia helped. A solid session for this holding.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google edged higher last night as AI regulation fears faded and tech bargain hunters stepped back in. There's ongoing debate about Google's $15 billion Malaysia data centre investment and whether the core search business is under threat from AI rivals, but for now the numbers still look solid.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two crept up last night with GTA 6 hype building — pre-order sales have reportedly hit $751 million with two weeks to go until release. Earnings are coming up and the marketing machine is in full swing. Positive momentum for this holding.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara was flat today — no movement at all. Lithium prices remain depressed and there's no fresh news catalyst. This one is down -58% overall from your cost base, which reflects how badly the lithium sector has been hit by oversupply and falling EV demand. The long-term thesis depends on a lithium price recovery.

watch_today.title: GTA 6 pre-orders hit $751M — TTWO momentum building
watch_today.detail: Take-Two's GTA 6 is reportedly raking in $751 million in pre-order sales with two weeks still to go before release. Earnings are coming soon and the marketing push is ramping up hard. Last night's small gain (+0.71%) reflects growing excitement. For a long-term holder, this is exactly the catalyst you've been waiting for — sit tight and let it play out.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX down -20% overall — AI regulation fear is the culprit
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF is under pressure as incoming US Democrat lawmakers signal a wave of AI regulation bills. The fund dropped another 2.71% today. That said, last night the NASDAQ bounced 1.09% as markets decided the regulation fears were overdone. If you believe in AI's long-term growth story, this dip could look like an opportunity in hindsight — but there's real short-term uncertainty here.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX still flat — lithium recovery is the only hope
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals didn't move today, sitting at $2.83 — down 58% from what you paid. There's no fresh news and lithium prices remain depressed. The long-term thesis (EV adoption driving lithium demand) is still alive but it's a waiting game. No reason to sell at these levels and lock in the loss unless you've given up on the thesis entirely.

watch_today.title: RBA cash rate now at 4.85% — watch mortgage and savings impact
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank has pushed the cash rate to 4.85%, with all four big banks (CBA, NAB, Westpac, ANZ) responding. This is relevant if you have a variable rate mortgage — repayments will be higher. On the flip side, savings rates are more attractive. Keep an eye on whether the RBA signals a pause or more hikes in coming weeks.

watch_today.title: Aussie dollar fell 0.91% — boosts your US holdings in AUD terms
watch_today.detail: The AUD dropped to US$0.6868 today. That's actually good news for your US holdings (GOOGL, MSFT, TTWO) — when you convert their value back to AUD, you get more dollars. It's a natural hedge. The flip side is imports get more expensive, adding to cost-of-living pressure.

watch_today.title: MSFT dipped but long-term story intact — hold steady
watch_today.detail: Microsoft slipped -0.99% last night despite the broader market rising. There's debate about whether its massive AI data centre spending will pay off, but the fundamentals remain strong and your position is still up nearly 20% overall. A single soft night is no reason to act.

world.summary: The big global stories today centre on the US political reshuffle after the midterms, an escalating Iran war with ongoing shipping incidents in the Gulf, and Israel's political shake-up.

stories.title: Trump names Stephen Miller as new White House Chief of Staff after midterm defeat
stories.why_it_matters: Donald Trump has replaced his chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller following the Republicans' losses in the US midterm elections. Miller is one of Trump's most hardline advisers — the architect of the administration's immigration crackdowns and a fiercely combative political operator. The BBC reports Trump is 'readying for a battle', suggesting a more aggressive, confrontational approach in Washington over the coming months. For markets, a more politically turbulent White House creates uncertainty around trade, immigration, and regulatory policy.

stories.title: Iran war escalation: risk remains high despite Democrat midterm sweep
stories.why_it_matters: Despite Democrats winning control of Congress in the midterms, analysts at CNBC warn the risk of the Iran conflict escalating remains high. The UAE has been rescuing crew from burning cargo ships in the Gulf of Oman — the latest being 22 crew members from a stricken vessel — highlighting how the conflict is already disrupting shipping through one of the world's most critical oil corridors. The Strait of Hormuz handles roughly 20% of global oil supply, so any escalation could spike oil prices and global inflation. Oil is already sitting at $90.83 a barrel.

stories.title: Israel President invites Gadi Eisenkot to form government
stories.why_it_matters: Israel's President has invited Gadi Eisenkot — a former IDF chief of staff and member of the National Unity party — to try to form a new government. This signals a potential political shift in Israel amid the ongoing Iran conflict, with a more centrist military figure being tapped to lead. Eisenkot has previously been a critic of some of Netanyahu's decisions, so this could represent a meaningful change in Israel's approach to the conflict and to ceasefire negotiations.

stories.title: Marco Rubio breaks silence on resignation rumours
stories.why_it_matters: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has spoken out to deny or address rumours that he is planning to resign from the Trump administration. Rubio has been a key figure in US foreign policy through the Iran conflict and Middle East tensions. Any instability at the top of US foreign policy leadership at this moment would be significant given the number of active flashpoints globally.

stories.title: Global travel set for record-breaking 2026 despite Middle East conflict
stories.why_it_matters: Despite the ongoing Middle East conflict, global travel is on track to hit record levels in 2026 according to The Independent. Consumer appetite for travel has proven remarkably resilient, which is good news for airlines, hotels, and tourism-related businesses globally. For Australians, this could mean continued pressure on airfare prices as demand stays strong.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 slipped 0.49% today to close at 9,020. Last night in the US, the NASDAQ jumped 1.09% and the S&P 500 edged up 0.31% as AI regulation fears quickly faded and bargain hunters bought back into chip stocks. Gold fell nearly 1% while oil was steady around $90.83. The Aussie dollar dropped 0.91% to US$0.6868.

indicators.note: Soft day on the local market — down 44 points.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session — modest gain as markets steadied.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Last night's session — solid rebound as AI regulation fears faded and chip stocks bounced.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil steady near $91 — Iran conflict keeping a floor under prices.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold pulled back slightly after recent strong run.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar fell — good for your US holdings in AUD terms, but adds to import cost pressure.

politics.summary: Domestically, the RBA's cash rate has hit 4.85%, WA Premier Roger Cook is fighting to protect the state's gas revenues, and the Albanese government is defending its decision to block a productivity review of industrial relations laws.

stories.title: RBA cash rate hits 4.85% — big four banks all respond
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank has lifted the official cash rate to 4.85%, and CBA, NAB, Westpac and ANZ have all responded — meaning variable mortgage rates will rise again for millions of Australians. This is the latest in a string of hikes aimed at bringing inflation under control. If you're on a variable home loan, your monthly repayments are going up. On the upside, term deposit and savings rates are also rising, which is good news for savers.

stories.title: WA Premier Roger Cook demands hands off gas and GST ahead of Senate vote
stories.why_it_matters: Western Australia Premier Roger Cook is pushing back hard against any federal moves to redirect WA's gas revenues or change the GST carve-up ahead of a critical Senate vote. WA has long argued it gets a raw deal from the GST formula. With federal budget pressures mounting, Canberra has been eyeing resource-state revenues. This fight could have significant implications for resource companies operating in WA and for how budget revenues are distributed nationally.

stories.title: Albanese government defends blocking productivity review of industrial relations laws
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is under fire for rejecting a Productivity Commission review of its industrial relations reforms — changes that have included multi-employer bargaining and strengthened union powers. Critics argue the government is avoiding scrutiny of laws that could raise business costs and reduce workforce flexibility. Business groups are frustrated, while unions and Labor argue the reforms are working as intended to lift wages.

ai.summary: The big AI story this week is the political tug-of-war in the US: Democrats' midterm wins have sparked fears of a wave of AI regulation, which briefly hammered tech stocks before markets calmed down. Meanwhile, Australian musicians are being pressured to re-record their own work so companies can legally own AI-training material.

stories.title: Democrats planning flood of AI regulation bills after midterm wins
stories.why_it_matters: Following the Democrats' sweep in the US midterm elections, Reuters reports they are preparing a large package of AI legislation for when they take control of Congress. This includes potential rules around AI transparency, liability, and use in elections. For tech companies like Google and Microsoft — which you hold — more regulation means more compliance costs and potential constraints on how they deploy AI products. Markets initially sold off hard on this news before partially recovering.

stories.title: AI safety advocates make gains after $110 million midterm fight
stories.why_it_matters: AI safety advocates — a group pushing for stricter controls on how powerful AI systems are built and deployed — spent $110 million backing candidates in the midterms and came out ahead, according to Bloomberg. This signals that AI regulation is no longer a fringe concern: it's becoming mainstream politics in the US. For AI-focused investments like your GXAI.AX ETF, this is the key risk to watch — tighter rules could slow the rollout of AI products and weigh on valuations of AI companies.

stories.title: Nasdaq rebounds 1.09% as AI regulation fears fade in a day
stories.why_it_matters: Just 24 hours after a sharp sell-off triggered by AI regulation fears, the NASDAQ bounced back 1.09% as bargain hunters piled into chip stocks. This kind of whipsaw reaction shows how sentiment-driven the AI trade is right now — fear of regulation can tank valuations in a day, then optimism brings them straight back. For long-term holders of AI-linked stocks, the volatility is uncomfortable but the underlying demand for AI computing power hasn't gone anywhere.

stories.title: Australian musicians pressured to re-record AI training tracks so firms can claim copyright
stories.why_it_matters: The AFR reports that Australian musicians are being pushed by tech and music firms to re-record their own existing tracks — not to release new music, but specifically so companies can own the copyright to AI training material. Because AI companies need massive amounts of audio data to train music-generating models, they want legally clean recordings they fully own. Critics say this exploits artists who are essentially being asked to sign away their creative work for AI development, often for minimal payment.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — Roosters 19, Knights 18 in an absolute nail-biter at Accor Stadium. Boxing also made headlines with a big fight result. The 2027 NRL season structure is already being mapped out.

stories.title: Roosters win NRL Grand Final 19-18 over Knights in a classic
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have claimed the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in one of the tightest Grand Finals in recent memory at Accor Stadium. Just one point in it at the final siren — the Knights will be gutted having come so close. It was a thriller right to the end and a great advertisement for the game.

stories.title: Ringside at NAS vs Gal — the haunting detail from fight night
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports has a first-person ringside account of the NAS vs Gal boxing bout, describing the experience as haunting. The piece suggests Gal was overpowered by NAS in what sounds like a one-sided result. The ringside detail — the sounds, the physicality, the emotion — is described as staying with the writer long after the final bell. No full article text available, but it was clearly a significant fight night.

stories.title: 2027 NRL season structure already being planned
stories.why_it_matters: With the 2026 Grand Final barely finished, Rugby League Zone reports that planning for the 2027 NRL season is already underway. This will likely include draw structure, potential expansion team decisions, and scheduling around international events. No specific details available from the article, but the NRL moves quickly — expect announcements about next season in the coming weeks.
